title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for carpet and upholstery cleaning
audience: Owners of carpet and upholstery cleaning businesses who want more work from households, agents, strata managers and public bodies that fit their service area and job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the work you do well (for example, steam cleaning of carpets and upholstery in houses), the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A block of flats or an office with regular carpet cleaning in your area is worth more than a single job across town. Business.gov.au suggests writing one short profile for each customer segment (24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Build a scored list of prospects
instruction.body: Keep one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. The criteria are the service area, the repeat need, whether there is a person who makes the decision, and whether the job falls within your insurance. Strata managers and real estate agents may be prospects, but the research did not find a source for their carpet buying, so check each one before you add it. Record the date and source of each contact detail. Do not buy or scrape lists: ACMA says buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

instruction.heading: Use public tenders and registers for businesses and public bodies
instruction.body: Public bodies buy cleaning services through tender systems. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026). AusTender lists federal opportunities and sends email notices. Neither was checked for carpet or upholstery work, so use them as places to look. Building permit data suits area-level planning, not individual contact (DataVic, 28 August 2026). Do not use any signal to target a private household.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message says how you found the business or notice, makes one verifiable observation (for example, a public listing or a published tender), and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area. Keep it honest and short. The ACCC found in July 2026 that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). Identify yourself and make it easy to decline.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the number of follow-ups and the gap between them in advance. Remove anyone who says no or asks you to stop, and record the request. ACMA says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. Each month, review which prospects replied and which turned into paid work.

procedure: Write the service, area, price range and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list, score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, and record the source of each contact detail.
Choose the public tenders and registers to check, and note the date each one is checked.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call Register and your insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of each month.

workedExamples.situation: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A solo carpet cleaner covers three suburbs. A public tender notice from a public body in one suburb asks for cleaning of carpeted areas in one of its buildings. The cleaner has not quoted for a public body before.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the tender a fit, and what should the cleaner do first?
workedExamples.reasoning: A public tender inside the service area is a business signal, not a private one, so it meets the criteria if the cleaner can deliver. Buying for Victoria lists tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026), so the cleaner can check the closing date and the requirements. Before deciding, the cleaner checks the licence and insurance the tender requires, because the research did not check them for carpet work. The cleaner does not contact building staff about the work outside the tender process. If the cleaner wants to make contact, the approach follows the electronic message and Do Not Call rules, and names the notice and one defined item.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to every prospect on a broad list.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong fits.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about a household to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person gave you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Bidding on work that needs a licence or insurance you do not hold.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the tender's requirements before you bid. Licence and insurance rules for carpet work were not researched.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix a number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence and insurance rules for carpet and upholstery cleaning were not researched. Check the rule for each state or territory where you work, and any tender's requirements, before you offer the service.

Commercial electronic messages are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent must be recorded, and that an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. The Act's text was not read for this lesson.
Check every telephone number against the Do Not Call Register before a telemarketing call. The 2018 DNCR industry guide gives the calling hours; check for updates before use.

Public listings and tender notices do not by themselves permit personal contact. The OAIC says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules where the Privacy Act applies. Coverage for a small business depends on turnover and other factors, and was not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the service, area and repeat need before you look for prospects.
Use public tenders and business registers as signals. Do not target private households from private information.
Gaps: no source for carpet buying by agents, strata managers or public bodies was found, and the tender portals were not checked for carpet work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A strata manager with several buildings inside your service area that you already visit
Any business with a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender for cleaning of carpeted areas is posted in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Check the tender's requirements, including licence and insurance, before you decide to bid
Message each resident in the building using their private details
Go into the building to look at the carpets before the closing date

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what must you do?
options: Make the message short enough to read on a phone
Confirm the consent and unsubscribe requirements in current ACMA guidance
Ask the prospect to like your social page first

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'How to identify your target market', https://business.gov.au/marketing/how-to-identify-your-target-market, 24 September 2024. Supports: write one short profile for each customer segment.

Buying for Victoria, 'How to get known', https://buyingfor.vic.gov.au/how-get-known, last updated 7 August 2026. Victoria. Supports: current and past tenders are listed; suppliers can set alerts; agencies publish annual procurement plans.

Department of Finance, 'Selling to Government' (AusTender guidance), https://sellingtogov.finance.gov.au/node/8, no date shown. Supports: suppliers can filter federal opportunities and receive email notices; awarded contracts of $10,000 or more are published.

DataVic, 'Building Permit Activity Data', https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/d397f0bc-d69b-4093-b8d5-d8daae4f73a3, last updated 28 August 2026. Victoria. Supports: permit records can be filtered by suburb or postcode, so they suit area-level decisions rather than individual contact. Owner and builder fields were not confirmed.

ACMA, 'Spam: Industry obligations', https://www.acma.gov.au/theACMA/spam-industry-obligations, last updated 28 March 2019 (older source). Supports: marketing messages need consent; an unsubscribe must work for at least 30 days and be honoured within 5 business days; publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages; buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

OAIC, 'Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-7-app-7-direct-marketing, page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019 (older source). Supports: public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules.

ACCC, 'Misleading and high pressure unsolicited sales practices widespread', https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/misleading-and-high-pressure-unsolicited-sales-practices-widespread, 28 July 2026. Supports: many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves.

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older source). Supports: telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm, not Sundays or public holidays; lists should be checked against the register.

ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04 per the research file. Supports: consent, accurate sender details, and an unsubscribe honoured within five working days.
Notes: no source in the research covers carpet buying by agents, strata managers or public bodies (gap). The tender portals were not checked for carpet work. The DNCR hours are from a 2018 guide.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: As recorded in the research files: consent is needed before marketing messages are sent; sender details must be accurate; each commercial message needs an unsubscribe that is honoured within five working days. Publisher: ACMA.
